snip.t: Inflammatory and autoimmune: Rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, Sjögren's
| Connective tissue disease–related | Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, SLE, myositis, Sjögren's |
CTD-ILD: commonly systemic sclerosis (NSIP), rheumatoid arthritis (UIP); treat with immunosuppression.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis: Coal dust — Coal miners — Small upper-zone nodules, progressive massive fibrosis, Caplan syndrome (rheumatoid arthritis + nodules)

Autoimmune disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis): Silica acts as adjuvant, breaking tolerance — Polyarthritis, skin thickening; may worsen pulmonary fibrosis — Can appear years after exposure; prevalence higher in silicosis
Topics tested: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, CREST and systemic sclerosis, myositis, vasculitis, gout and pseudogout, osteoporosis and fibromyalgia.

qs.q: What is the typical female-to-male prevalence ratio for rheumatoid arthritis?
qs.e: Rheumatoid arthritis affects females more frequently than males with a ratio of 3:1. Other ratios listed do not reflect the epidemiology described in the text.

qs.q: Which of the following genetic factors is specifically noted to be associated with rheumatoid arthritis?
qs.e: Genetic predisposition for rheumatoid arthritis is necessary and is associated with HLA-DR4. HLA-B27 is characteristically linked to seronegative spondyloarthropathies rather than RA.

qs.q: During the cellular pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis, which cells primarily compose the joint fluid?
qs.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory cells invade the synovium and fluid, with the joint fluid being mostly composed of neutrophils. Other white blood cells do not make up the primary cellular component of the fluid.

qs.q: Which cytokine is highlighted as playing a pivotal role in the inflammatory and destructive processes of rheumatoid arthritis?
qs.e: IL-1 plays a pivotal and crucial role in the inflammatory and destructive processes of RA, leading to phenomena like cartilage and bone destruction. The other interleukins listed do not share this specific primary destructive role in the text.

qs.q: Which classic joint involvement is characteristically spared in rheumatoid arthritis?
qs.e: RA classically presents as symmetrical polyarthritis involving various joints EXCEPT the DIP joints. Joints like the MCPs and PIPs are frequently affected in rheumatoid hands.

qs.q: What is the classic duration that distinguishes morning stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
o: More than one hour in rheumatoid arthritis versus less than half an hour in osteoarthritis
Less than fifteen minutes in rheumatoid arthritis versus several hours in osteoarthritis
Exactly thirty minutes in both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis conditions
Only upon heavy exertion for both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis conditions
qs.e: Morning stiffness is prolonged in rheumatoid arthritis lasting more than one hour, whereas in osteoarthritis it lasts less than half an hour. Shorter durations are not characteristic of active rheumatoid inflammation.

qs.q: What does a Baker's cyst behind the knee in a rheumatoid arthritis patient potentially put them at risk for developing?
qs.e: A Baker's cyst can compress vascular structures, setting up conditions for a DVT to develop, which requires a quick assessment. The other complications listed are not directly caused by vascular compression from a popliteal cyst.

qs.q: A patient with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic syndrome. Which rare complication of prolonged active disease is the most likely cause?
qs.e: Amyloidosis is a rare complication of prolonged active disease in RA and usually presents with nephrotic syndrome in the form of proteinuria. RA by itself does not cause direct primary glomerulonephritis.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune synovitis causing joint damage and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern, serology and imaging; early treatment prevents disability.

sections.p: RA is a symmetric polyarthritis with persistent synovial inflammation. Diagnosis uses the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria: joint involvement, serology (RF, anti‑CCP), acute‑phase reactants, symptom duration.
b: RF or anti‑CCP positivity increases specificity

t.b: Does the patient have autoantibodies? Positive result supports autoimmune etiology and predicts erosive disease
Is there erosive change? Joint space narrowing and marginal erosions confirm established disease
Is there active synovitis? Detects early inflammation when X‑ray is normal

sections.p: Disease activity is graded by DAS28 or CDAI; radiographic staging (Sharp/van der Heijde) tracks erosions. Functional status uses HAQ.
RA is multifactorial: genetic predisposition (HLA‑DRB1), smoking, and mucosal citrullination. In low‑resource settings consider co‑existing infections that can trigger or mimic RA.
b: TB or hepatitis B can cause reactive arthritis

sections.p: Patients report morning stiffness >30 min, symmetrical small‑joint swelling, fatigue, and systemic features (fever, weight loss). Extra‑articular: rheumatoid nodules, lung disease, vasculitis.
Combine history, exam, serology and imaging to confirm and monitor disease.

t.b: Is inflammation active? Elevated levels indicate active disease and guide treatment intensity
Any interstitial lung disease or nodules? Detects Caplan syndrome or RA‑ILD
Could infection mimic RA? Positive test prompts alternative diagnosis

sections.p: Rapid joint destruction, pulmonary nodules (Caplan), interstitial lung disease, vasculitis, amyloidosis, infection from immunosuppression.
b: New lung symptoms in a miner → Caplan

sections.p: Treat the autoimmune process, control inflammation, protect joints and monitor complications.
b: Start a csDMARD (e.g., methotrexate) as first‑line
Add a bDMARD if disease remains active
Avoid long‑term NSAIDs alone due to GI/renal risk

sections.p: Regular DAS28 assessment every 3‑6 months, X‑ray every 1‑2 years, vaccination, smoking cessation, physiotherapy, osteoporosis prophylaxis.
b: Bone density scan after 6 months of steroids

sections.p: Seronegative RA and normal acute‑phase reactants can occur, especially early disease.
b: Negative RF/anti‑CCP does not exclude RA
CRP may be normal in low‑grade inflammation

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe joint swelling with fever
New onset dyspnoea or cough in a miner (possible Caplan)
Signs of infection while on immunosuppressants
